Administrative: PO Box 12846 • Austin, TX  78711 • Email: admin@aanp.org • Website: aanp.org 
Government Affairs: 1400 Crystal Drive, Suite 540 • Arlington, VA  22202 • Email: governmentaffairs@aanp.org 
September 2, 2025 
The Honorable Douglas A. Collins 
Secretary of Veterans Affairs 
Department of Veterans Affairs 
 
RE: Reproductive Health Services 
Dear Secretary Collins,  
The American Association of Nurse Practitioners (AANP), representing more than 431,000 nurse 
practitioners (NPs) in the United States, appreciates the opportunity to provide comment on the 
Department of Veterans Affairs proposed rule on reproductive health services. AANP is concerned that as 
written the rule could limit access to care because of the physician certification requirement.  
As you know, NPs are advanced practice registered nurses who are prepared at the masters or doctoral 
level to provide primary, acute, chronic and specialty care to patients of all ages and backgrounds. Daily 
practice includes assessment; ordering, performing, supervising and interpreting diagnostic and laboratory 
tests; making diagnoses; initiating and managing treatment including prescribing medication and non-
pharmacologic treatments; coordinating care; counseling; and educating patients and their families and 
communities. NPs hold prescriptive authority in all 50 states and the District of Columbia (D.C.) and 
perform nearly one billion patient visits annually. Currently, twenty-seven states, the District of Columbia 
and two U.S. territories have adopted full practice authority (FPA), granting patients full and direct access 
to nurse practitioners.1 
 
NPs practice in nearly every health care setting including VHA facilities, hospitals, clinics, Indian Health 
Services facilities, emergency rooms, urgent care sites, private physician or NP practices (both managed 
and owned by NPs), skilled nursing facilities (SNFs) and nursing facilities (NFs), schools, colleges and 
universities, retail clinics, public health departments, nurse managed clinics, homeless clinics, and home 
health care settings. As you are aware, since December of 2016, NPs have been authorized to practice to 
the full extent of their clinical education and training within VHA facilities. According to the VA “[d]ata 
demonstrates that FPA for APRNs has a positive impact on wait times in Mental Health, Specialty Care 
and Primary Care.”2  
Importantly, removing barriers for NPs was a policy objective of President Trump’s first Administration. 
We strongly support Section 5 of Executive Order 13890 on Protecting and Improving Medicare for Our 
Nation’s Seniors, which called for removing burdensome requirements in the Medicare program that are 
“more stringent than applicable Federal or State laws require and that limit professionals from practicing 
at the top of their profession.8 Additionally, the Reforming America’s Healthcare System Through Choice 
and Competition report from the Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Treasury, 
and the Department of Labor9 called for removing barriers on APRNs. HHS also released a Rural Health 
Strategy Report during President Trump’s first term that highlighted removing practice barriers on NPs as 
a key activity to support the rural health workforce.3  
 
Under this proposed rule, the CHAMPVA benefit package exclusion for abortions at § 17.272 would 
revert back to language that states that abortions are excluded “except when a physician certifies that the

2 https://www.va.gov/budget/docs/summary/fy2024-va-budget-volume-ii-medical-programs.pdf.

Government Affairs: 1400 Crystal Drive, Suite 540 • Arlington, VA  22202 • Email: governmentaffairs@aanp.org 
life of the mother would be endangered if the fetus were carried to term.”4 In instances where the patient 
is receiving treatment from a nurse practitioner or other qualified clinician, or a physician is not available, 
this could lead to unnecessary delays in treatment that could jeopardize the life of the mother.  
 
As noted in this proposed rule, VA guidance already includes an exception where abortions are covered 
as a maternity care service when “the life or health of the pregnant Veteran would be endangered if the 
pregnancy were carried to term”5 As noted in that directive, VA maternity care services must be provided 
by “qualified providers” defined as “a licensed medical practitioner operating within the scope of their 
license.”6 Similarly, authorized non-VA providers within the CHAMPVA program to provide covered 
medical services and supplies are generally providers that are “licensed or certified by a state to provide 
the medical services and supplies.”7 Consistent with these provisions, and in accordance with state law, 
we strongly recommend that the VA use similar language in § 17.272 and replace “physician” with 
“qualified provider.” This would create consistency across the programs, align the policy with state law, 
and improve access to treatment for mothers in medical emergencies.   
 
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule and we look forward to continued 
partnership with the VA. Should you have comments or questions, please direct them to MaryAnne 
Sapio, V.P. Federal Government Affairs, msapio@aanp.org, 703-740-2529.  
 
Sincerely, 
 
Jon Fanning, MS, CAE, CNED 
Chief Executive Officer 
American Association of Nurse Practitioners
